b: Compiled from the course folder (UET Peshawar, 3rd semester CED lectures)
Plan (noun): a physical representation (drawing/map) OR an orderly arrangement of parts of an objective.
Planning: deliberately achieving an objective by assembling actions into an orderly sequence.

Planning as general activity: making an orderly sequence of action leading to stated goals; techniques = written statements, statistical projections, mathematical representations, quantified evaluations, diagrams; may (not must) include physical blueprints.
Urban planning: planning with a spatial/geographical component; aims at a spatial structure of activities (land uses) better than without planning.
Also called: physical planning; "spatial planning" is the more neutral, precise term.
Urban/regional planning is a special case of general planning that includes the plan‑making (representational) component (Hall, 2002).
Urban planning integrates land use planning + transportation planning to improve built, economic and social environments.
Urban renewal: applying planning methods to existing cities suffering decay and lack of investment.
Planned city: planned from inception, usually on previously undeveloped land; fewer land‑use conflicts.
Communities constantly change through development and population growth — planning controls rather than reacts.
Planners prepare socio‑economic and physical design plans based on residents’ felt needs.
Aims: preserve/enhance quality of life, protect physical & natural environment, promote economic growth.
Stakes: planning decisions involve large sums of public/private money; deliver large gains to some and losses to others.
Challenges: in a democratic society planning is tied to politics, law, economics and ideology.
Best planners: master the technical side AND have "peripheral vision" — understand links with political, social, demographic and economic forces.
Rural settlement too small to be a village
Larger than a village, smaller than a city
Relatively large, permanent settlement; complex sanitation, utilities, land use, housing, transport; often has legal/administrative status
Separate residential community within commuting distance of a city
Ring of prosperous communities beyond the suburbs; commuter towns
Mainly residential; most workforce commutes out
Dense urban core + less‑populated surroundings sharing industry, infrastructure, housing
Higher population density and human features than surroundings (cities, towns, conurbations)
Several cities/towns merged by growth into one continuous urban‑industrial area
Term by geographer Jean Gottmann (1961) for cities of the US northeast seaboard growing into one urban region
Joel Garreau (1991): commercial centres growing far outside the old central city (e.g., Tysons Corner)
Cities grow outward from the centre in a series of rings.
Context: 1920s, class‑conscious society, housing segregated by income, poor transport.

Assumptions: older buildings in centre, newer at edge; land values highest in centre; strong economic/ethnic segregation; low‑income groups lack transport so live near centre; flat plain with equal access.

Five zones: (1) CBD; (2) Transition & industry — low income, oldest housing, ghettos; (3) Low‑income residential; (4) Middle‑income residential — suburban estates, gardens; (5) High‑income residential/commuter — small towns & villages.
Criticism: old; ignores car ownership, landscape, effect of industry & transport; zones never so clear‑cut.
Sectors radiate out from the CBD along transport routes.
Context: late 1930s; income/status‑divided society; housing reflects social segregation.
Assumptions: growth along transport routes; low‑income and industrial areas lie next to each other; wealthy choose best sites.
Criticism: old, too general; most zones have mixed uses; ignores urban renewal.
Burgess vs Hoyt: Hoyt based on statistical data → less open to criticism.
City develops around several business centres (nuclei), each a growth point; growth spreads until nuclei merge.
Modern cities more complex than earlier models; a mixture of Burgess and Hoyt.
Some uses attract similar uses (industry); some repel others (housing away from industry).
Criticism: not an exact fit for all cities; too complex.
Some relevance only; urban renewal puts high‑income housing near CBD.
Modern cities expand beyond these models → urban sprawl.

chapters.t: History of City Design & Urban Growth

s.t: Five pre‑industrial ideas of city design
b: Wall: defence/fortification; later the idea of limits to the city.
Grid: easy to map and subdivide land; Greeks in Asia Minor (~500 BC); Spanish colonial cities (e.g., Lima).
Axis: emphasises important places/people (Beijing imperial axis; Pope Sixtus V in Rome linking monuments).
City square: "living room" of the city; began as markets; green squares in England/N. Europe.
Cloister: sacred spaces (monasteries, temples, churches) in prominent locations.
Chang’an (Xi’an), China: largest city c. 800 AD (>1 million), Tang capital; walls ≈ 9.7 × 8.6 km, 11 gates, central axis, grid; prototype for Beijing.
Bastides (France, 12–13th c.): fortified grid new towns; market square at centre (e.g., Monpazier).
Rome (16th c.): Sixtus V — axes, view corridors, piazzas (Piazza del Popolo); led to St Peter’s Square — icon of Baroque planning.
London fire 1666: Wren & Evelyn plans not used, but influenced the New World.
Philadelphia (William Penn / Thomas Holme): grid, two main streets, five squares; "green country town".
Adelaide (Col. William Light): surrounded by a greenbelt; North Adelaide added as separate town.
Washington DC (L’Enfant): grid + monumental axes; later best example of City Beautiful movement.
Growth sequence (Kansas City): riverboats & wagons → railway → street railways (suburbs along lines) → automobile (spread anywhere).
By 1950 three of four US households owned cars.
Metropolis split into old city (pre‑1950) and new suburban city with its own offices/shopping (edge cities).
Sprawl became dysfunctional: congestion, long commutes, car dependence → revival of walkable downtowns.
Remedy: transit linking new‑city centres to old CBD; multi‑city "mega‑regions" forming worldwide.

chapters.t: Sustainable Development & Urban Planning in Pakistan
b: Brundtland Report (Our Common Future): development that meets present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet theirs.
UN‑Habitat (1996) sustainability measures: quality of life, scale of non‑renewable resource use, recycling/re‑use, renewable resource use, waste produced and its environmental impact.
Pakistan system: planning & housing departments at federal, provincial, local level; development authorities in big cities (CDA, RDA, LDA, KDA); 3‑tier local government under PLGO 2001.
Islamabad master plan prepared by Doxiadis Associates (1960).
Housing schemes developed without approval; mere land subdivision into residential/commercial.
Green area 0.85–2.19% vs prescribed ≥7%; public buildings 0–0.41% vs 5–10%; graveyard 0% vs ≥2%.
Green standard fell: 3 acres/1000 persons (1970 plan) → 1 acre/1000 (1996 plan); actual 0.69 acre/1000 (1996).
Amenities 2–7 km away → more car trips, fuel, emissions.
Water shortage and poor quality (diarrhoea, stomach infection); untreated sewage into nullahs; sewers in only ~35% of city.
Open dumping of solid waste; non‑conforming uses (schools, clinics, parlours in houses).
National figures cited: housing shortage 7.57 million units (2011); ~25% urban population in squatter settlements; sewerage for only 48%.
Local bodies to prepare and approve urban & environmental development plans; strong development control.
Uniform planning & environmental standards; simplify EPA clearance.
Public participation; independent periodic evaluation of plans.
Comprehensive solid waste management; engineered landfill + composting; source segregation (kitchen vs other waste).
Sewage treatment plants; water metering and conservation; use of solar energy.
Walkable/cycleable neighbourhoods; green areas at sub‑neighbourhood level; public‑private partnership and cross‑subsidy for projects.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Planned cities of Pakistan: Islamabad — master plan by Constantinos Doxiadis (1960s), grid of sectors (e.g., F-6, G-9) with a dynapolis concept; Lahore Development Authority, CDA, KDA (Karachi), PDA (Peshawar) control planning.

Urbanisation: Pakistan’s urban population ≈ 37–40% (census-based), with rapid growth of Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Rawalpindi–Islamabad and Peshawar; informal settlements (katchi abadis) are common.
Islamabad’s master plan: Doxiadis; Chandigarh: Le Corbusier; Brasília: Lúcio Costa & Oscar Niemeyer.

chapters.t: Role of Transportation in Urban Planning
b: Transportation = mobility of people and goods; a basic human need; shaped human civilisation and settlement (recall land‑use theories).
Planner’s inputs: solution must be analytically based, economically sound, socially credible, environmentally sensitive, practically acceptable.
Technology: from bus/rail only to LRT, MRT (e.g., Manila LRT, Jakarta/Singapore MRT).
Public values: identify target groups (rich, poor, young, work/leisure trips).
Suburbanisation complicates collection (getting rider to vehicle) and distribution (vehicle to destination).
Trade‑off: wider stop spacing → higher speed but poorer access.
Ideal environment: jobs concentrated in core + apartments near stops (large, older cities); high density discourages car use.
Demand‑response (para‑transit, e.g., Dial‑a‑Ride): vehicle sent on call; no fixed route or schedule; biggest growth area.
Forecasting: estimating future vehicles/people using a facility (road, rail line, airport, seaport).
Purpose: infrastructure capacity (e.g., number of lanes), financial & social viability, project impact.
Classical Four‑Stage Model (FSM): Trip generation → Trip distribution → Modal split → Traffic assignment.
Street network: connected roads made of nodes and segments.
Node: intersection of two or more streets, or end of a street.
Segment: line connecting two nodes; Link = segment with direction (Lij from i to j).
Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ): study area divided into zones instead of points.
Trip: movement >300 m from origin to destination with a purpose; vehicle trip vs person trip; two trip ends.
Design capacity: max vehicles passing end of a link per time without delay (veh/h).
Design speed: max speed on a link with no delay; higher on flat than steep roads.
Rows = origins; last column = total trips produced by each zone.
Columns = destinations; last row = total trips attracted to each zone.
Diagonal = intra‑zonal trips. Zone attracting most trips likely an employment/shopping centre.
Free flow; low volume, high speed
Reasonably free / stable flow; some speed restriction
Stable flow; speed and lane changes controlled by volume
Forced flow / breakdown; queuing; volume exceeds capacity
Predicts total trips produced by and attracted to each zone ("how many trips?").
Depends on: zone population, income, vehicle ownership; also household size, age distribution, education, occupied dwelling units.
Expressed as trips/employee, trips/unit land area, trips/occupied dwelling unit.
Methods: growth factor model, regression model, category (cross‑classification) analysis.
Growth factor: Ti = fi × ti; fi = f(Pd, Id, Vd) / f(Pc, Ic, Vc) (d = design year, c = current year).
Growth factor overestimates → used mainly for external trips; regression preferred for internal trips.
Regression: Y = a + b1X1 + b2X2 + … (multiple linear regression), coefficients by regression analysis.

Worked example (growth factor): 275 households with car (5 trips/day) + 275 without (2.5 trips/day). Current trips = 1375 + 687.5 = 2062.5. If all get cars: fi = 550/275 = 2.0 → future = 4125 trips/day. Realistic estimate = 550 × 5 = 2750 trips/day → shows growth factor over‑estimates.
Trip distribution: where trips go; gravity model based on Newton’s law of gravitation; growth factor method responds only to relative growth rates at origins and destinations.
Modal split: share of trips by mode (public vs private); logit — equal utilities give equal probability (0.5 each).
Traffic assignment: selection of routes between origin and destination in the network.
Urban transportation planning: the process leading to decisions on transport policies and programmes.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Gravity model: Tij = Pi Aj f(cij) / Σ Aj f(cij) — trips decrease with travel impedance (distance/time/cost).
Order: trip generation → trip distribution → modal split → traffic assignment.
LUA studies where and what human activities take place on land; tells if land suits an activity and the consequences of change.
Land cover: natural and human‑altered land surface on which activities take place.
Land utilisation (land use): the activity/action on the land.
LUA is carried out where change is expected. Answers: what to build, where, when & how, and what impact.
In short: how land is used now, what changes are allowed under rules, impacts of those changes.
Intensity of use (activity per unit area)
Interrelations (access affects use; links to employment, income, investment)
Special interest groups: environment, economic development, farming — analyse impacts on their interests.
Suitability = land has the features to support a proposed use (social, physical, spatial, economic factors). Factor categories:
Access: distance to roads, surface water, sewer and water lines.
Select factors and their attribute values.
Identify available land from existing uses.
Compare with comprehensive plan/zoning to remove unavailable land.
GIS is used to overlay factor maps and compute weighted suitability (Assignment 4 topic).
Cities occupy ~2% of land but use ~75% of resources and produce ~70–80% of CO₂/GHG emissions.
Largest CO₂ emitters: buildings, energy and transport — hence greatest mitigation potential.
Six investments for green cities: low‑carbon transport, green industry, energy‑efficient buildings, city greening, green resilient infrastructure, intelligent systems.
Compact, dense, mixed‑use cities are most resource‑efficient (e.g., Singapore); low‑density sprawl raises energy use and excludes the poor.
Four spatial models: monocentric (radial trips, needs mass transit), polycentric (random trips), "urban village" (live near work), composite (most common).
WHO: 9 m² green space per capita within 15‑minute walk.
Tools: 3R (reduce–reuse–recycle), TOD (transit‑oriented development), BRT, rainwater harvesting, green roofs, LEED rating.
Land‑use regulation types: minimum plot size, FSI/FAR limits, zoning, subdivision rules.
Art and science of designing and erecting buildings and other physical structures.
Style and method of design and construction; buildings and large structures; orderly arrangement of parts.
Practice of the architect (professional services for built environment).
Vitruvius (Roman, ~25 BC): firmitas, utilitas, venustas → "Commodity, Firmness and Delight" (Sir Henry Wotton, 1624).
More than shelter — a cultural artifact; "a projection of a society on the ground".
Material: depends on resources; shape linked to technology and workforce.

s.t: Le Corbusier — "A house is a machine for living in" (Villa Savoye)
b: Free plan — structure separated from walls; rooms flow.
Pilotis — building raised on columns; away from damp, open to light and air.
Ribbon windows — continuous horizontal windows, broad views.
Roof terrace — flat roof as usable outdoor space.
Idea precedes object; communicated by sketches, plans, sections and elevations.
Examples: BMW Central Building (Zaha Hadid — "nerve centre"); Jewish Museum Berlin (Libeskind).
Famous works cited: Pyramids of Giza, Step Pyramid of Zoser, Parthenon, Acropolis, Stonehenge, Chartres Cathedral, Machu Picchu.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Classical orders: Doric (plain, sturdy), Ionic (scroll/volute capitals), Corinthian (acanthus leaves); Tuscan and Composite are Roman additions.
Mughal & Islamic architecture in Pakistan: Badshahi Mosque & Lahore Fort (Mughal), Shalimar Gardens (charbagh layout), Wazir Khan Mosque (kashi tile work), Faisal Mosque (modern, by Vedat Dalokay).
Principles of design: Unity, balance (symmetrical/asymmetrical), proportion & scale, rhythm, emphasis, contrast, harmony; Le Corbusier’s Modulor based on golden ratio (≈ 1.618).
‘Form follows function’ — Louis Sullivan; ‘Less is more’ — Mies van der Rohe; Fallingwater — Frank Lloyd Wright.

By level: national, regional, master/comprehensive, local/neighbourhood, site plan.
By duration: short‑term (≤5 yr), medium (5–10 yr), long‑term/perspective (20+ yr).
Planning elements: land use, transport, housing, utilities, community facilities, open space, economy, environment.
Related professions: architecture, civil engineering, economics, law, sociology, geography, environmental science.
Planner’s functions: survey & analysis, plan preparation, development control, public consultation, policy advice, implementation & monitoring.

s.t: Garden city, satellite town, squatter settlements
b: Garden City: Ebenezer Howard (1898/1902); self‑contained town ~32,000 people surrounded by a greenbelt; combines town and country (Letchworth, Welwyn).
Satellite town: smaller town near a big city to absorb its overflow, partly dependent on it (e.g., Rawalpindi’s Satellite Town).
Squatter settlement (katchi abadi): informal housing on land not owned by occupants; upgrading = regularising tenure + providing water, sanitation, roads.
Climate change: long‑term change in climate due mainly to GHG emissions; responses = mitigation (cut emissions) and adaptation (cope with impacts).
Urban heat island: city hotter than surroundings due to paving, buildings, less vegetation, waste heat; remedy — trees, green/cool roofs, water bodies.
Rainwater harvesting: collect roof/surface runoff for storage or groundwater recharge.
Sources: residential, commercial, institutional, industrial, construction & demolition, municipal services.
Functional elements: generation → storage → collection → transfer & transport → processing/recycling → disposal (sanitary landfill).
ISWM: integrated hierarchy — reduce, reuse, recycle, recover (compost/energy), then dispose.
Pakistan: mostly open dumping, low collection efficiency, large organic fraction suitable for composting.
Principles: truth/purpose and beauty. Qualities: strength, vitality, grace, breadth, scale.
Features: domes, minarets, arches, courtyards, geometric and calligraphic ornament (e.g., Badshahi Mosque, Taj Mahal).

Each A-size is half of the previous one; sides in ratio 1 : √2.
Pencils: H series = hard (9H hardest), B series = soft (9B softest), HB = medium. Typical use: 2H construction lines, H dimension lines, HB outlines & lettering.
T-square: horizontal lines. Set squares (45° and 30°–60°): vertical/inclined lines; together give angles in multiples of 15°.
Divider: transfers distances / divides lines. French curves: irregular curves. Mini-drafter: replaces T-square, set squares and protractor.
Dimension, extension, leader, hatching (section) lines, short centre lines, imaginary intersection lines
Centre lines, axes, lines of symmetry, pitch circles
Chain thin, thick at ends & bends
Adjacent parts, extreme positions of moving parts, centroidal lines
Precedence when lines coincide: visible > hidden > cutting plane > centre line > break line > dimension/extension > hatching.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 14.1 — Types of lines and their uses.
Visible outlines: continuous thick; hidden edges: dashed; centre lines: thin chain; cutting plane: chain thick at ends & bends.
Single-stroke letters, vertical or inclined at 75° to the horizontal.
Type A: stroke thickness = h/14. Type B: stroke thickness = h/10.
Main title 7–10 mm; sub-titles 5–7 mm; dimensions and notes 3.5–5 mm.
Lower-case letter height ≈ 0.7 h; spacing between characters ≈ 2 × stroke thickness.
Elements: dimension line, extension (projection) line, arrowhead, leader line, dimension figure/note. All drawn thin.
Extension line: small gap (~1 mm) from object, extends ~3 mm beyond dimension line.
First dimension line ~10 mm from outline; next ones ~8 mm apart.
Aligned system: figures parallel to dimension line, readable from bottom or right side, placed above the line.
Unidirectional system: all figures read from the bottom; dimension line is broken for the figure.
Arrangement: chain (continuous), parallel, progressive (from a common datum), combined.

Rules: units in mm (unit not written); each feature dimensioned once; avoid dimensioning hidden lines; never use an outline or centre line as a dimension line; place dimensions outside the view; smaller dimensions inside, larger outside.
Symbols: Ø diameter, R radius, SØ sphere diameter, SR sphere radius, □ square.
Representative Fraction (RF): drawing length ÷ actual length (same units). RF > 1 enlarging, = 1 full size, < 1 reducing.
Length of scale = RF × maximum length to be measured.
Area RF = (linear RF)²; volume RF = (linear RF)³.
Reads two units (e.g. m & dm) or one unit and its fraction
Reads three units (e.g. m, dm, cm); based on similar triangles; reads to 1/100 of main unit
Reads two units; small divisions read using least count
Two scales with same RF but different units (e.g. km & miles)
Used by pattern makers (allows for metal shrinkage)
Least count (vernier): 1 MSD − 1 VSD = MSD ÷ number of vernier divisions.
Direct vernier: VSD < MSD (n VSD = n−1 MSD). Retrograde vernier: VSD > MSD (n VSD = n+1 MSD).
Typical civil scales: building plan/elevation/section 1:100 or 1:50; details 1:20, 1:10, 1:5; site plan 1:200–1:500; key/location plan smaller.

s.t: Conic sections (cone cut by a plane)
b: Inclined to axis, cuts all generators
Eccentricity: distance of point from focus ÷ distance from directrix.
Ellipse: sum of distances from the two foci = major axis. Distance from focus to end of minor axis = half major axis.
Ellipse methods: concentric circles, rectangle (oblong), arcs of circles, trammel, eccentricity, parallelogram, four-centre (approximate; used in isometric).
Parabola methods: rectangle, tangent, eccentricity. Uses: arches, reflectors, projectile path, BM diagram of simply supported beam under UDL, cable under UDL.
Hyperbola uses: cooling towers, PV diagram. Rectangular hyperbola (asymptotes at 90°): xy = constant, e.g. Boyle’s law PV = C.
Cycloid: path of a point on a circle rolling on a straight line; base length = πD.
Epicycloid: circle rolls outside another circle. Hypocycloid: rolls inside; becomes a straight line when rolling circle Ø = ½ directing circle Ø.
Trochoid: point inside (inferior) or outside (superior) the rolling circle.
Involute: path of the end of a string unwound from a circle/polygon; used for gear tooth profiles (cycloids also).
Archimedean spiral: equal radial movement for equal angular movement (cams, scroll chucks). Logarithmic spiral: ratio of successive radius vectors constant (equiangular).
Helix: point moving around a cylinder/cone and along its axis uniformly; pitch = axial advance per turn. Uses: screw threads, springs, spiral staircases.
Regular polygon: interior angle = (n − 2) × 180° / n. Hexagon side = radius of circumscribing circle.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 18.1 — Conic sections: ellipse, parabola and hyperbola.
Other curves: Cycloid (point on rolling circle), epicycloid/hypocycloid (circle rolling outside/inside another), involute (gear teeth), Archimedean spiral (cams), helix (springs, screw threads).
Eccentricity: e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola; rectangular hyperbola (asymptotes ⊥) describes Boyle’s law pV = constant.
Projectors parallel to each other and perpendicular to the plane of projection; observer at infinity.
Planes: HP (horizontal), VP (vertical), PP (profile, ⟂ to both). XY line = intersection of HP and VP (reference line).
Views: Front view/Elevation on VP; Top view/Plan on HP; Side/End view on PP.
Above HP, in front of VP
Below HP, in front of VP
First angle: object between observer and plane. Top view below front view; left side view on the right of front view. Used in Pakistan, India (BIS), UK, Europe.
Third angle: plane between observer and object. Top view above front view; left side view on the left. Used in USA, Canada.
2nd & 4th angles not used: front and top views overlap.
Projection symbol: two views of a truncated cone (frustum).
Two views usually enough for simple objects; three for most; cylinder can be shown in one view with Ø.
Auxiliary views: AVP (⟂ HP, inclined to VP) gives auxiliary front view; AIP (⟂ VP, inclined to HP) gives auxiliary top view. Used to get true shape of inclined surfaces.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 19.1 — Arrangement of views in first-angle and third-angle projection.
First angle: object between observer and plane (top view BELOW front view); third angle: plane between observer and object (top view ABOVE front view).
Point h above HP and d in front of VP (1st quadrant): front view a′ is h above XY; top view a is d below XY; aa′ ⟂ XY.
Point on HP: front view on XY. Point on VP: top view on XY.
Line ∥ to both HP & VP: both views true length (TL), ∥ to XY.
Line ⟂ HP: top view is a point; front view TL, ⟂ XY. Line ⟂ VP: front view is a point.
Line ∥ VP, inclined θ to HP: front view = TL showing true θ; top view shorter, ∥ XY.
Line inclined to both planes: neither view TL; apparent angles α > θ and β > φ.
θ + φ ≤ 90°; θ + φ = 90° when the line lies in a profile plane.
Finding TL & true inclinations: rotating line method, trapezoid method, auxiliary plane method.
Traces: HT = point where line (extended) meets HP; VT = meets VP. A line ∥ to a plane has no trace on it.
Plane ∥ HP: top view = true shape; front view = line ∥ XY.
Plane ∥ VP: front view = true shape; top view = line ∥ XY.
Plane ⟂ both HP & VP (profile plane): both views are lines ⟂ XY; side view true shape.
Plane inclined θ to HP, ⟂ VP (AIP): front view = line at true θ; top view = reduced shape.
Oblique plane (inclined to both): no view shows true shape; solved by change-of-position (2/3 stage) or auxiliary plane method.
Platonic solids (5): tetrahedron (4 △), cube (6 □), octahedron (8 △), dodecahedron (12 pentagons), icosahedron (20 △).
Solids of revolution: cylinder (rectangle about one side), cone (right triangle about one ⟂ side), sphere (semicircle about diameter).
Right solid: axis ⟂ base. Oblique solid: axis inclined to base.
Frustum: part left after cutting by a plane ∥ base. Truncated: cutting plane not ∥ base.
Axis ⟂ HP: start with top view (true shape of base). Axis ⟂ VP: start with front view.
Sphere: every view is a circle of the same diameter.
Cutting plane line: thin chain, thick at ends and bends, arrows show viewing direction, labelled (A–A).
Hatching: thin lines at 45° to main outline, ~1–3 mm apart; adjacent parts hatched in opposite direction or different spacing.
Not sectioned when cut lengthwise: shafts, bolts, nuts, rivets, keys, pins, ribs, webs, spokes, balls.
Types: full, half (¼ removed; symmetric objects), offset (stepped cutting plane), broken-out/partial, revolved, removed, aligned, auxiliary.
True shape of section: obtained on a plane ∥ to the cutting plane.
Section of cylinder by inclined plane = ellipse; any section of a sphere = circle.
Material hatching (civil): brick masonry 45° lines; concrete dots + small stones; earth irregular strokes; timber grain lines; stone masonry irregular blocks; glass thin diagonal strokes.
Unfolding all surfaces of a solid onto one plane in true size; always uses true lengths.
Uses: sheet-metal work (ducts, hoppers, chimneys, funnels, tanks, trays).
Methods: parallel-line (prisms, cylinders), radial-line (pyramids, cones), triangulation (transition pieces), approximate (sphere — zone/lune method).
Cone lateral surface: sector of radius L (slant height) and angle θ = 360° × r / L.
Pyramid: triangles about apex, radius = true length of slant edge.
Curve/line where two solids interpenetrate; found by line (generator) method or cutting-plane method.
Two equal cylinders with axes intersecting at 90°: intersection appears as straight lines in front view.
Three axes at 120°; on paper two axes at 30° to horizontal, one vertical. Each axis inclined 35°16′ to plane of projection.
Isometric projection: uses isometric scale. Isometric drawing/view: uses true lengths (≈ 22.5% larger).
Only isometric lines (∥ to axes) show measured lengths; non-isometric lines are located by end points.
Circles appear as ellipses (four-centre method). Sphere: circle of radius = true radius in isometric projection, 1.22 × radius in isometric drawing.
Axonometric types: isometric (3 equal angles), dimetric (2 equal), trimetric (all different).
Front face ∥ to picture plane shown in true shape; receding lines at 30°, 45° or 60° (usually 45°).
Cavalier: receding lines full scale. Cabinet: receding lines half scale (more realistic).
Keep circular features and longest dimension ∥ to picture plane.
Projectors converge to the observer’s eye (station point); most realistic; used by architects.
Terms: Station Point (SP), Picture Plane (PP), Ground Line (GL), Horizon Line (HL), Vanishing Point (VP), Centre of Vision.
Objects farther away appear smaller; parallel lines meet at vanishing points.

Isometric scale: Isometric length ≈ 0.816 × true length (cos 35°16′); isometric drawing uses true lengths, isometric projection uses reduced lengths.
Oblique: Cavalier: receding lines full scale at 45°; cabinet: receding lines half scale.
Isometric axes are 120° apart (30° to horizontal); perspective uses vanishing points (one-, two-, three-point).
Plan: horizontal section through doors/windows (around sill–lintel level, ~1–1.5 m above floor) viewed from above.
Section: vertical cut from foundation to roof; usually taken through staircase, doors, windows and WC.
Drawing order: plan first → elevation projected from plan → section.
Site plan: plot boundary, building position, roads, services, north direction. Key/location plan: site relative to surroundings.
North line usually shown on plan; levels shown as RL.
Other drawings: foundation plan, working drawings, detail drawings, structural (RCC detailing, bar bending schedule), plumbing, electrical layout.
Openings notation: D door, W window, V ventilator, CW clerestory window.
Plumbing symbols: WC, wash basin, sink, floor trap, gully trap, inspection chamber, manhole.
Electrical symbols: switch, socket, light point, fan, distribution board (DB).

Abbreviations: RCC, PCC, DPC (damp-proof course), GL (ground level), NGL (natural ground level), PL (plinth level), FFL (finished floor level), RL (reduced level), BM (bench mark), c/c (centre to centre), NTS (not to scale).
Coordinates: absolute (x,y); relative (@x,y); polar (@distance<angle). Angles measured anticlockwise from +X (east = 0°).
Draw commands: LINE, PLINE, CIRCLE, ARC, RECTANG, POLYGON (3–1024 sides; inscribed/circumscribed), ELLIPSE, SPLINE, HATCH, TEXT/MTEXT.
Modify commands: MOVE, COPY, ROTATE, SCALE, MIRROR, OFFSET, TRIM, EXTEND, FILLET (R = 0 gives sharp corner), CHAMFER, ARRAY (rectangular/polar/path), STRETCH, BREAK, JOIN, EXPLODE, ERASE.
ZOOM/PAN: change only the display, not object size. SCALE changes actual size.
File types: .dwg drawing, .dwt template, .dxf data exchange, .bak backup.
Others: LIMITS, UNITS, LAYER, BLOCK/WBLOCK/INSERT, model space vs paper space (layouts, viewports), PLOT.
